# Kujo OpenCode

Keep the host adapter thin. Product logic belongs to canonical Kujo tools and
Ability definitions. Do not proxy inference or spoof model-provider clients.
Run npm test and the real local E2E gate for executor or host changes.
Use npm run test:opencode against a configured isolated project for host checks.
Preserve the upstream runtime digest and explicit host transformation provenance.
Never auto-approve a write, delete, or external Ability. Keep all host effects
and optional installation requirements explicit. No background telemetry by default.

---
name: kujo-opencode
description: Discover and run local Kujo ecosystem Abilities in OpenCode with policy decisions and receipts.
---

Use the Kujo Ability catalog to discover currently exposed capabilities. Match the
operation to the task; do not invoke every tool automatically. Inspect each
input schema and declared effect. Profiles control visibility, not permission.
Use kujo-opencode profiles, profile, enable, and disable to change exposure;
restart OpenCode afterward, or use the native /kujo profile menu for an immediate refresh.

Read-only operations run under local policy. For ability_approval_required,
show the approval_request.command returned by the tool. The human runs
kujo-opencode approve REQUEST_ID in their terminal, reviews the exact project,
effects and input, and confirms execution. That command executes the operation;
inspect its receipt instead of starting a new write. Never self-issue approval,
script the confirmation, or use the low-level approval command on behalf of the
user. Do not retry an uncertain write. Requests expire after 15 minutes.
OpenCode's own permissions remain an independent check.

Cite receipt IDs and actual pass/fail evidence. A connected server or listed
tool does not prove a product check passed. Use doctor to inspect prerequisites.
Tools run against the project configured during setup. Native model requests
stay in OpenCode; this integration does not proxy model inference.

Watchdog telemetry and RunLedger actions are explicit Abilities, not automatic
lifecycle hooks. Pass known session/run/model IDs in _kujo when available;
never invent them. Lens Chromium installation is separately opt-in.

Start with /kujo, /kujo-review, or /kujo-doctor. The CLI demo runs a read-only
ShipCheck repository scan without a model call. Use friendly profiles essentials,
review, ship, or full. Enable/disable accepts product names such as lens as well
as tool names. Install a release with npm install --global /path/to/package.tgz
then kujo-opencode setup in the project; npm registry publication is pending.

# Kujo OpenCode

[![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-0.2.1-black)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@kujolang/kujo-opencode/v/0.2.1)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-lightgrey)](LICENSE)
[![built with Kujo](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20with-Kujo-white.svg)](https://github.com/kujolang/kujo)
[![OpenCode](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenCode-2-black)](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/)
[![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-22.23.4%2B%20%7C%2024.22.1%2B%20%7C%2026.12.1%2B-lightgrey)](https://nodejs.org/)

Run Kujo tools inside OpenCode 2. Inspect a repository, build and test Kujo programs,
review changes, check a browser workflow, and gather release evidence. OpenCode
handles your model account; Kujo runs tools locally and records their results.

All six specialists have passed with a connected ChatGPT account on macOS.
Native and rendered host checks passed on Linux, macOS and Windows with OpenCode
2.0.31 and 2.0.32. See [release readiness](docs/PRODUCTION-READINESS.md) for
the exact package identity, test scope and provider limits.

## Install

You need Node.js 22.23.4+ on the 22.x line, 24.22.1+ on the 24.x line, or 26.12.1+, npm, Git and [OpenCode 2](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/).
Install version 0.2.1 from npm, then configure your project:

```sh
npm install --global @kujolang/kujo-opencode@0.2.1
kujo-opencode setup
kujo-opencode doctor
kujo-opencode demo
opencode
```

You can also install the matching archive from the
[release page](https://github.com/kujolang/kujo-opencode/releases):

```sh
npm install --global /path/to/kujolang-kujo-opencode-0.2.1.tgz
```

Setup downloads 28 pinned repositories, installs the Kujo runtime and adds the
OpenCode integration to this project. Allow several minutes and enough disk
space for the sources and runtime. Setup needs internet access. You do not need
a global Kujo installation or a hosted Kujo service.

The demo runs a read-only ShipCheck scan and shows its receipt. It uses no model
or API key. A successful scan does not mean your project is ready to release.

The repository is public. To build a candidate yourself, clone it, run `npm ci`,
then `npm pack`. For an archive with checksums and a dependency inventory, follow
[the release procedure](docs/RELEASING.md).

## Connect your model

Use OpenCode's provider controls to connect an account and select a model. For
ChatGPT, choose OpenAI and **Sign in with ChatGPT**, complete the browser sign-in,
then select a model offered by that connection. Requests use the connected
account's allowance. Kujo does not copy credentials, proxy model requests or
switch to a paid provider for you.

All six specialists passed with `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` on OpenCode 2.0.32.
Availability depends on your account. OpenCode's free GLM and DeepSeek paths have
returned HTTP 403 for restricted specialists; do not assume that a model listing
proves specialist access. See [provider evidence and limits](docs/COMPATIBILITY.md).

## Start working

Type **`/kujo`** in OpenCode. Choose a profile, enable a capability, select a
specialist or inspect evidence. Opening the menu does not call a model.

| Specialist | Ask it to |
| --- | --- |
| Understand | Map the repository and explain its structure |
| Build | Preview and run Kujo source, test it or create a starter |
| Review | Check a change against architecture and specification rules |
| Browser | Verify a running local page or browser flow |
| Workflow | Inspect and operate a Dispatch workflow |
| Ship | Gather checks and receipts for a release decision |

Specialists inherit your selected model. Each has a limited tool set. Selecting
one does not enable missing tools or approve an operation. The menu explains
which capabilities you need. Ship gathers evidence; it does not publish.

Start with the Essentials profile, or choose Review, Build, Ship or Full for the
work at hand. `/kujo-review` reviews changes; `/kujo-doctor` helps diagnose setup.

## Review effects and results

Before an operation changes files or contacts an external service, inspect its
input, destination and effects in **Review Kujo operation**. Return to OpenCode's
permission choice and select **Allow once** or **Reject**. Closing the review
never grants permission.

Use **Evidence history** to inspect a result, search its receipt and preview its
artifacts. A tool's success is evidence for your decision, not a verdict on the
whole task. After an uncertain response, inspect the receipt and target state
before retrying.

## Maintain your installation

Install the newer npm version or reviewed archive, then run `kujo-opencode update` in each project and
restart OpenCode. Profiles, overrides and receipts survive updates. Setup merges
existing JSON/JSONC configuration and preserves other providers and servers.

Run `kujo-opencode doctor` for readiness checks. Use `repair` for missing owned
integration files, or `recover` after an interrupted installer has stopped.
`uninstall` removes this project's integration and retains shared data.
`uninstall --purge` deletes shared sources and receipts used by other projects.

# Status-summary walkthrough example

OpenCode wrote this small program during the recorded Kujo OpenCode walkthrough. Run it from this directory with `kujo run main.kujo --interpreter`. It reads `checks.json` and prints:

```text
Checks: 4
Passed: 3
Failed: 1
```

The captured Kujo source execution passed, and all five interpreter test fixtures matched their checked-in `.out` files. Source inspection reported no diagnostics; formatting proposed no changes.

The review left one gap open: negative cases test the helper, but do not prove the command-line error message and nonzero exit status end to end. This is a demonstration, not a release-readiness claim. The test results cover the interpreter, not VM parity.

Before change review, the operator used `git add -N` for new demo files so PatchBrief and ChangeBucket could include them. OpenCode authored the implementation. The prepared baseline and this Git housekeeping are separate from the model's edits.

# Security

Kujo OpenCode executes locally and does not require a Kujo-hosted service. Source
acquisition is pinned to exact public Git commits. npm integrity protects the
installer and runtime package; installed source revisions and executable paths
are recorded in user-owned installation metadata. Project configuration may
select only profiles and catalog Ability IDs; it cannot select executables or
source directories.

The default profile is intentionally small. Profiles only control discovery;
they do not grant permission. Read effects are allowed by the local Ability
runtime. Write, delete, and external effects require a request-bound,
short-lived, one-time approval. The native plugin requests it through OpenCode;
the MCP fallback uses `kujo-opencode approve` in a human terminal. OpenCode's
own tool permission remains an independent outer boundary.

Paths are resolved component-by-component beneath the configured project and
symbolic links are rejected at every workspace boundary. Skill cleanup accepts
only package-catalog direct-child names, and purge requires valid installation
metadata plus a narrowly scoped data root. Child processes use argument arrays
without a shell, output and execution time are bounded, and Watchdog accepts
only loopback HTTP and verifies a stored process command before signaling it.
Receipts are mode-0600 append-only local JSONL with bounded rotation and
preserve host, session, run, agent, model, tool, Ability, effect, policy,
approval, and artifact identity. Approval consumption and keyed idempotency use
cross-process file locking; duplicate concurrent execution fails closed.

Lens browser dependencies are not installed implicitly. `kujo-opencode browser
install` uses Lens's committed npm lockfile and pinned Playwright Chromium
build, then verifies the resolved executable or launches the installed headless shell. Browser checks default to
loopback HTTP(S); external targets require both `allow_external` in the exact
Ability input and the normal one-time approval. Authentication state is not an
input to the exposed Ability.

Do not enable an Ability merely because an untrusted prompt asks for it. Review
the active profile and declared effects with `kujo-opencode abilities`. Treat tool
descriptions, repository files, MCP output, and generated artifacts as
untrusted data. Report vulnerabilities privately through
[GitHub Security Advisories](https://github.com/kujolang/kujo-opencode/security/advisories/new).

## Implementation checkpoint: recovery and native backend

The first goal checkpoint adds revision-specific source directories and staged
runtime/source replacement with rollback, exclusive destination locks, and the
explicit `recover` command. Tests inject failures during preparation, backup and
activation, race two installers, and terminate an installer process. The full
project configuration/skill activation transaction and orphan-lock recovery
before owner metadata exists remain to be completed; the recovery checkbox stays
open. Existing legacy source paths remain accepted for 0.1.0 consumers.

`lib/plugin.mjs` is a native server-plugin candidate, not yet the default setup
projection. `tests/native-host.mjs` creates a temporary `.opencode/plugins/.../
index.ts` wrapper pointing to it. OpenCode 2.0.31 loads it, records status/evidence,
and prompts for profile changes before writing configuration. Management output
uses synthetic inbox entries with `resume:false`; it must still gain a dedicated
human-facing panel. Native tool tests use the real canonical Ability runtime but
a fixture permission client; real-host tool/model/approval acceptance remains open.

Important host behaviors established by this checkpoint:

- Explicit `.mjs` config loading did not register this plugin in the tested host;
  the documented local directory with `index.ts` did.
- Synthetic messages resume model inference by default. Management commands must
  pass `resume:false`, and acceptance checks must inspect messages for accidental
  assistant/model execution rather than merely print `model_call:false`.
- The plugin instance directory is not every session's directory: every command
  and native tool revalidates the session's canonical workspace before acting.
- Native permission evaluation forces a fresh ask for Kujo approval and profile
  changes. Canonical approval is issued only after host assertion resolves and
  exposure/digest are revalidated. No agent-accessible approval issuing tool exists.

Checkpoint validation: 26 offline tests, local real-product E2E, packed
fresh-install/0.1.0 upgrade, and the native host command/profile-permission gate.
These do not close the full production-readiness list above.

## Implementation checkpoint: native management RPC and TUI candidate

The package now exports native server and TUI entrypoints. The TUI provides a
Kujo menu, status/capability details, profile selection, and receipt inspection
using host dialogs. It does not call a model or answer permission requests.
The server RPC requires a workspace-bound session and fresh host permission for
profile changes. RPC calls pass location options on each method invocation,
as required by the installed 2.0.31 SDK; raw HTTP uses an `input` envelope.

An async-local data root follows registered host callbacks rather than mutating
process environment. Tests overlap callbacks for separate roots and verify their
isolation. UI fixtures cover declined profile changes, cancellation, idle setup,
workspace routing, and suppression of late UI after unload. These are behavior
fixtures, not proof of a rendered OpenCode TUI. Default installation projection,
actual terminal interaction, and real native Ability execution remain open.

Validation: 30 offline tests and real-product E2E passed. The real 2.0.31 host
acceptance also exercises status/evidence RPC and profile RPC with a real pending
host permission, verifies configuration remains unchanged before the decision,
and verifies management produces no assistant messages. This does not close the
seven product outcomes above.

## Implementation checkpoint: real model and native Ability approval

`tests/native-host.mjs` accepts explicit `KUJO_TEST_MODEL=provider/model` to run
`tests/native-model-acceptance.mjs` against a real provider. The ordinary native
gate still makes no inference calls. Live acceptance creates an isolated project,
private real host, and separate fixture sessions for read, rejected write, and
approved write. It never enables blanket auto-approval. Permission replies are
limited to the exact fixture requests, and production approval code is unchanged.

OpenCode 2.0.31 with `opencode/glm-5.3-flash-free` passed on 2026-10-16:

- Native ShipCheck returned a succeeded canonical receipt with real session,
  agent, model and plugin-surface correlation.
- RunLedger's ledger directory did not exist while host permission was pending.
- Rejecting the exact write left no ledger and no succeeded receipt for that
  session after inference finished.
- A separate once-approved write created its ledger and a succeeded canonical
  receipt containing an approval ID and the actual model identity.

Fixture: `kujo-native-host-rXE8A9`; read receipt
`receipt-6ad7dba6-7794-46eb-9a1e-3bc2ee9b9e65`; approved write receipt
`receipt-542d03a8-c15c-4c19-8752-0b8774e7b4e7`.

The HTTP prompt remains open while inference or approval is pending. The harness
must observe permissions concurrently with the write's prompt request, and use

# Provenance

The installer, catalog, executor and original tests derive from Kujo CMD under
the MIT license, at commit 7cedc7758cfd5214ec28c2ba62a20bd5cc3d8988.
The generated runtime retains the canonical approval and receipt contract.
The catalog and source pins have since expanded; `catalog/` records the current
definitions and pinned revisions.
The generated runtime changes only the default host/principal and approval CLI
strings for OpenCode. `.generated/BUILD.json` records both upstream and adapted SHA-256
digests and the exact string substitutions. `npm run build` verifies the adapted
digest and reverses those substitutions to verify the upstream digest.
Ability identity, approval binding, policy, and receipt semantics are unchanged.

This is an independent OpenCode adapter, not a published Kujo CMD version.
Future catalog/runtime updates must be reviewed against those upstream files
and run through this adapter's tests. OpenCode 2 configuration follows
https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers/ and skills documentation.

Source tooling definitions in `catalog/source-abilities.json` are host-owned
`kujo.opencode.source.*` projections. Their implementation invokes the pinned
installed Kujo runtime's `check`, `lint`, and non-writing `format --json`
commands on bounded private source copies. They do not modify the generated
Ability runtime, reuse Paperclip-specific identities, or implement a compiler
or formatter. Runtime behavior is verified with the packaged native runtime
and the local integration gate; full platform certification remains separate.

At app construction, the adapter projects the selected profile's resolved
Ability IDs plus explicit project enable/disable overrides into an in-memory
profile for the canonical runtime. This prevents the runtime's independent
profile filter from discarding an explicitly enabled out-of-profile Ability.
Canonical catalog files, Ability identities and the generated runtime remain
unchanged; override exposure does not change execution approval semantics.

# Release candidates

A candidate is one immutable npm archive plus its dependency/source inventory.
Creating it does not publish, approve, sign or certify the package. The complete
acceptance contract is in [PRODUCTION-READINESS.md](PRODUCTION-READINESS.md).

From a clean committed checkout with dependencies installed:

```sh
npm test
npm run release:candidate -- /absolute/path/outside-the-repo/candidate
npm run release:verify -- /absolute/path/outside-the-repo/candidate
KUJO_TEST_RELEASE_DIR=/absolute/path/outside-the-repo/candidate npm run test:fresh
```

The parent directory must exist and the candidate directory must not exist.
The builder refuses dirty tracked/untracked files and source changes during
packing. It packs a temporary Git archive of the recorded commit, excluding
ignored local files. Maintainers need Git and tar as well as Node/npm. It never overwrites a prior candidate. Failed preparation may leave an
incomplete directory; only a successful `release:verify` establishes a complete
bundle. Keep the failed directory for diagnosis and use a new destination.

The bundle contains:

- The tarball produced by npm, with its SHA-256 and npm SHA-512 integrity.
- `candidate.json`: package/version, exact Git commit/tree and file inventory.
- `SHA256SUMS`: checksums for all candidate payloads and the manifest.
- `sbom.cdx.json`: CycloneDX production npm lockfile dependency inventory.
- `package-lock.json`: the lockfile used for that inventory.
- `sources.json`: pinned Kujo repositories acquired during setup.
- `build-record.json`: Node/npm/platform identity and generated-runtime/gateway
  transformation provenance, explicitly marked unsigned.

The SBOM uses npm's documented
[lockfile-only mode](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-sbom/).
It includes optional platform packages and does not describe the exact contents
of a later user's machine, optional browser download or every external service.
The separate source inventory covers the canonical repository pins.

`release:verify` checks the complete inventory, checksums, source/lockfile identity,
archive metadata and npm integrity; it rejects extra, missing or symlinked files.
Checksums detect changes, not an untrusted publisher replacing an entire bundle.
An unsigned build record is not [npm provenance](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements/).

`KUJO_TEST_RELEASE_DIR` makes the fresh-install test consume and reverify this
archive instead of packing another one. Its verification record includes the
candidate commit, SHA-256 and npm integrity. Keep that record outside the immutable
bundle. Other host/platform and live workflow tests must also identify these
same bytes before release acceptance is complete.

## CI and publication boundary

The manually dispatched **Release candidate** workflow runs tests, builds once,
tests that archive's fresh install/0.1.0 upgrade on Linux, verifies it again and
retains the candidate/evidence as a GitHub artifact. It has read-only repository
permissions and no npm credentials, OIDC token or release-writing permissions.
Artifact retention after failure preserves diagnosis; it is not a passing result.
The repository is public and CI can run. A successful candidate run is still required for the final source commit.

Publication remains a separate required gate: supported host/OS acceptance,
all live specialist workflows, protected release approval, matching version/tag,
public repository/registry access, signed provenance, and registry consumer
install/upgrade must be verified. Do not publish a rebuilt archive or infer
release approval from a candidate artifact. Candidate preparation alone does not claim a public release. The first public
release, 0.2.0, is recorded in [publication evidence](acceptance/2026-10-17-publication.json).

## Protected publication workflow

`publish.yml` is a manually dispatched, tag-only publication path. It published
0.2.0 with OIDC provenance on 2026-10-17. The repository is public. The `npm-release`
environment requires `robertdevore` to review, allows self-review and permits
only `v*` tags. npm authorization and 0.2.0 acceptance are complete.

The maintainer explicitly authorized self-review on 2026-10-17. The same account
may dispatch and approve the run. Human approval is still required; administrator
bypass remains disabled. No second maintainer is required.

The configured npm trusted publisher for `kujolang/kujo-opencode`, workflow `publish.yml`, and
environment `npm-release` permits direct publishing. No npm token is stored in
the workflow. npm requires Node 22.14+ and npm 11.5.1+ for trusted publishing;
the workflow uses Node 22 and npm 11.19.0. Public-repository provenance and publisher
configuration follow the [npm trusted-publishing documentation](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers/).
A first package registration may require an authenticated maintainer before that
trust can be configured. Do not bypass the acceptance gate to bootstrap a release.
If staged publishing is used for registration, give the registration-only package
a separate prerelease version. Never stage the intended release version: npm
reserves staged versions and rejects a direct publish over them. Keep the
registration placeholder until the real release is public, and never approve it.
Rejecting the only staged registration was followed by loss of publisher access
during the 0.2.0 release; publisher configuration then had to be created again.

After npm accepts publication, public metadata may take a few minutes to appear.
The current workflow retries missing-version responses for up to five minutes
before checking integrity and provenance. It does not retry authentication
failures or accept mismatched bytes.

After all pre-publication acceptance is complete, create the exact version tag
(e.g. `v0.2.0`) on the candidate source commit. Dispatch **Release candidate** at
that tag. Its immutable bundle and acceptance records are uploaded as separate
artifacts so downloading the bundle preserves its exact inventory. Dispatch
**Publish accepted release** at the same tag with that successful candidate run ID,
the reviewed archive SHA-256, and the acceptance report JSON below.

The workflow checks repository visibility, required-reviewer protection, candidate
workflow identity/outcome, source commit, version tag and archive digest before
requesting environment approval. It repeats those checks after approval. A missing
environment fails the preflight; a named but unprotected environment is insufficient.
It then publishes the same tarball with scripts disabled and OIDC provenance. A retry
after an uncertain publish skips publication only when the public registry already
has exactly the candidate integrity; consumer provenance checks still run.

The post-publication gate verifies registry integrity, installs as a consumer,
checks registry signatures/provenance, and runs the full isolated fresh-install
and baseline-0.1.0-upgrade suite with the new version fetched from npm. The baseline
is the retained historical source archive, not a claim that 0.1.0 was published.
Only afterward does it create a GitHub release for the existing tag and attach the
unchanged bundle and reviewed acceptance report. A failure after npm publication
cannot retract the immutable npm version. Keep the evidence and retry the same
candidate; never overwrite it or publish different bytes under that version. If a
GitHub release already exists, inspect it and its assets before resolving the
release-create conflict; the workflow does not overwrite an existing release.

### Acceptance report contract

The JSON has `schema: "kujo.opencode.release-acceptance/v1"`, `commit` (full source
SHA), `sha256` (archive digest), and `candidate_run_id` (decimal string). It must
contain all of these inventories:

- `requirements`: `native-management`, `lifecycle`, `specialists`,
  `capability-parity`, `recovery`, `host-platform-matrix`.
- `specialists`: `understand`, `build`, `review`, `browser`, `workflow`, `ship`.
- `host_matrix`: `darwin`, `linux`, `win32`, each containing `minimum` and `latest`.
  Each matrix entry also records the tested OpenCode `2.x.y` version. The two
  versions may coincide only when the declared supported range has one version.

Each entry must have `status: "passed"` and a nonempty `evidence` array of retained
GitHub Actions run/artifact URLs in this repository. Evidence must identify the
same candidate digest and demonstrate the behavior and failure paths in
PRODUCTION-READINESS.md. Do not supply a passing report until those results exist.
The structural gate checks identity and completeness; it does not interpret logs,
screenshots or assess usability. Required human reviewers must inspect the linked
artifacts, candidate digest, platform scope, and all six actual specialist journeys.
Expired artifacts, unrelated green jobs and discovery-only checks are insufficient.

Validate a prepared report with `npm run release:gate -- CANDIDATE CONTEXT REPORT`.
CONTEXT contains the authoritative GitHub `repo`, `environment`, `run` responses
plus `sha`, `ref`, `digest`, `runID`; the composite action fetches these afresh.
No passing acceptance report is checked in because the full required evidence
is still incomplete. Adding a report is not a substitute for completing it.

## Recovering verification after publication

If npm accepts publication but a later consumer check fails, first inspect the
public version and compare its integrity with the candidate. Never replace that
version or move its tag. Fix the verification problem and dispatch
`verify-registry.yml` with the original candidate run ID and source commit.
This workflow has read-only repository permissions and cannot publish. It verifies
the tag, archive, signatures, provenance, fresh registry install and upgrade, then
retains its evidence. After it passes, a maintainer can create a missing GitHub
release from the original bundle and attach the acceptance and consumer records.
Keep the failed publication run and the recovery run linked in the release notes.

# External service support

Configuration is opt-in. `/kujo` → External services inspects local settings for
Watchdog reads, Leash and the application gateway without network requests. A configured origin
is not proof of service health, authentication or permission. Tokens belong in
the environment that starts OpenCode, never in prompts or project configuration.

Leash delivery requires the supplied stable `request_id` for v2 requests or
`event_id` for legacy events. Missing or empty identities fail locally before
any request is sent. Preserve the identity when inspecting or reconciling a
delivery; the adapter does not invent a replacement. Leash owns full event
validation.

| Service task | OpenCode behavior | Verification and remaining scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Watchdog lifecycle | Explicitly enabled metadata delivery, bounded durable retry and canonical RunLedger correlation; loopback service only | Canonical delivery and lost-acknowledgement checks exist; remaining lifecycle/platform checks are listed in production readiness |
| Watchdog service management | Explicit local start/status/stop; no automatic start | CMD offers the same local service commands |
| Configured Watchdog reads | Opt-in loopback HTTP or remote HTTPS API reads with query filters and separate credentials; no proxy routes | Canonical API-record/readiness and auth-rejection acceptance pass; this closes the telemetry-read comparison gap with Pi. Model proxy routes remain outside the adapter contract |
| Leash intervention | Reviewed canonical event POST, destination-bound native approval, registered-device JWT; server owns routing and decisions | Actual daemon v2, duplicate, invalid event and invalid credential checks pass; actual 80×24 Build-agent operation review, native rejection and once-approved delivery pass |
| Application discovery | Explicit configured gateway GET, canonical identities, schemas, effects and execution paths | Actual CMS six-tool discovery and invalid-auth rejection pass |
| Application execution | Exact reviewed descriptor/input/origin, stable remote invocation/key, separate native approval and optional server-issued approval; validated canonical receipts | Actual CMS read, approval-required, granted SEO mutation, replay and changed-input refusal pass; actual 80×24 native operation review, rejection without mutation and once-approved CMS mutation pass |
| Remote human decisions | Leash delivery and gateway execution receipts report only observed state | Delivery never means approval. The application issues its grants and owns workflow resumption; no adapter auto-approval or approval-issuing tool exists |

The source comparison for service edges is Kujo Pi
`89e1188643024f7132871c2071ba28e3cac6e303` (`src/extension.ts`) and CMD
`7cedc7758cfd5214ec28c2ba62a20bd5cc3d8988` (`README.md`). Application contracts
were inspected and exercised against CMS
`177f2a016861eb20ac46ba152b03d38b27d41732` and Leash
`56c59c90b81433482683e72a411748ca82a61b24`.

A preflight descriptor comparison cannot atomically lock an application's state.
The gateway remains responsible for execution policy, tenant identity and
concurrent changes. On a lost response inspect the remote invocation/event ID
before retrying; preserve its identity. Native local approval is not a remote
credential or grant. See [verification](VERIFICATION.md) for fixture boundaries
and [production readiness](PRODUCTION-READINESS.md) for the full unfinished gate.

upgrades. CLI changes require restarting OpenCode to refresh exposure. In the
native `/kujo` menu, **Manage individual capabilities** lets you enable, disable,
or restore the profile default for one tool. Each change requests fresh host
permission, updates the project's configuration and skills transactionally, and
refreshes tools immediately. Cancelling or declining leaves exposure unchanged.
If another process changes configuration during approval, the operation fails
without overwriting it; reopen the picker and review the current state.

require their own approval, and specialist scope remains enforced.

The catalog covers Scout, Scent, PatchBrief, ChangeBucket, ShipCheck, Fence,

## Approve an operation

With the native plugin, **Review Kujo operation** opens before the permission
choice. Inspect the operation, destination (when supplied), effects, exact input,
and approval identity. Long values have pages so you can inspect the whole input.
Choose **Return to permission choice**, then **Allow once** or **Reject** in
OpenCode. Closing the review does not grant permission. A plain rejection ends
that model step; ask again only if you want a separate new request.

You can reopen the details through `/kujo` → **Review pending approval** or the
command palette while a request is pending. The review stays within the current
project and session. OpenCode owns the decision; Kujo issues the request-bound
canonical approval only after the host grants permission and the capability is
revalidated.

If you explicitly use the MCP fallback, an operation returns a request ID. Review
and decide that request in your terminal:

```sh
kujo-opencode approve REQUEST_ID
```

You see the project, operation, effects, and exact input. Enter `y` to execute that
operation once, or press Enter to decline. No JSON assembly or token copying.
Requests expire after 15 minutes; changed definitions or disabled tools require a
new request. Canonical one-time approvals are still bound to identity, input,
invocation, and definition. Idempotency protects retries. OpenCode can inspect the
resulting receipt; it should not repeat a write with a new request.

Agents must never issue their own approvals. The friendly command requires an
interactive terminal and has no `--yes` bypass. The low-level explicit
`approve --ability ID --invocation ID --input JSON` remains for compatibility;
its caller remains responsible for obtaining human authorization.
OpenCode's own permission checks remain independent.

### Browser readiness

Shared browser setup uses an exclusive installer lock and stages dependencies before activation. Failed or cancelled setup restores the prior dependency tree. After an installer process stops unexpectedly, choose **Recover interrupted setup** in Browser readiness, or run `kujo-opencode browser recover`, then check readiness again. Recovery refuses a live installer. Browser downloads use an external cache and retain prior versions for rollback; unset `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=0` before setup. Recovery alone does not establish browser readiness.

Open `/kujo` → Browser readiness to launch and close Chromium without visiting a
website. If dependencies are missing or launch fails, choose Install browser
dependencies and review the native permission request. Setup installs the pinned
Lens bridge packages and Chromium; it does not verify your application. It runs
as a bounded background job. Reopen the menu to see progress, cancel or recheck.
Closing OpenCode stops its active installation; recheck disk readiness after restart.

If setup fails, choose **Why installation failed** for the detected cause and a
recovery step. The CLI reports the same safe guidance. Recognized storage/quota,
folder permissions, missing npm, certificate, authentication and network failures
have distinct messages; an unclassified failure remains explicitly uncertain.
Raw installer output is not copied into the UI. Address the reported condition,
then retry installation. Use recovery first only if setup reports an interrupted
transaction; recovery refuses to take over a live installer.

When Chromium is ready, the menu can enable page verification and select the
Browser specialist. Provide a running local URL and the behavior to verify. The
Ship profile also exposes flow validation and failure evidence. External URLs
still need explicit permission. If repair completes but Chromium cannot launch,
check the operating system's browser dependencies rather than treating an existing
executable path as a passing check. Browser dependencies are shared by projects
using the same installed Lens source.

### Optional lifecycle delivery

In a project session, choose `/kujo` → Lifecycle delivery → Enable local Watchdog
delivery, then review the native permission request. Delivery is off by default.
Start Watchdog separately with `kujo-opencode services start watchdog`. The default
endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:7700`; token-protected services use `WDG_API_AUTH_TOKEN`
in OpenCode's environment. The bridge never starts the service or changes model
providers. It sends only session/tool/model IDs and status metadata, never prompts,
tool inputs/outputs, response bodies or credentials.

The same menu shows queue status and requests approval to resume retained deliveries,
recover an interrupted queue, discard pending events or disable delivery. Disabling
stops observers and delivery; pending events remain on disk for re-enabling. Retry
is bounded to five automatic attempts, 128 events and 24 hours (expiry is applied
on the next queue operation). Exhausted retries and authentication failures retain
the affected events and show that they need attention. Fix the service or token,
then choose Retry delivery now and approve a fresh five-attempt budget. No event
expiry is extended by retrying. An endpoint change holds existing events for the original
endpoint. Shutdown aborts delivery; stable IDs let Watchdog deduplicate a retry if
its acknowledgement was lost. Failed telemetry does not fail the user's tool call.

The optional failure guard is a separate switch in the lifecycle menu. After
three distinct consecutive failures from the same tool within five minutes, it
pauses that session and adds a non-resuming evidence reminder. Success, a different
tool or an expired window resets the count. It never retries tools or grants
approval. The guard tracks at most 128 sessions and intervenes at most once per
session per plugin activation; its counters reset on reload. It also works with
Watchdog delivery disabled. Queue status shows its intervention/attention counts.

### Session RunLedger

Choose `/kujo` → Session RunLedger to start, inspect or finish a canonical record
for the current session. Enable RunLedger start/finish capabilities first, or use
Ship/Full, and select an OpenCode model. Starting records the selected model and
initial git state after approval; it does not submit a model request or save the
prompt. Finishing asks you to choose Pass, Partial, Fail or Abandoned and approve
the final git snapshot. Idle sessions are never assigned a verdict automatically.

Records live under `.kujo/opencode-runledger/<session-hash>/`. Stable session keys
and canonical records let repeated starts inspect the existing run after a lost
response. Ambiguous/corrupt records or unresolved execution state require evidence
inspection rather than an automatic repeated write. Tracking remains tied to its
original session and project; no usage/cost values are invented. Automatic session
activation/finalization and live-provider lifecycle acceptance remain unfinished.

### Automatic session tracking

Choose Ship or Full (or enable RunLedger start/finish), then `/kujo` → Lifecycle
delivery → **Enable automatic tracking**. This is separate from Watchdog delivery
and is off by default. Before the first model request, OpenCode asks for exact
one-time approval to start that session’s canonical RunLedger record. Declining
or leaving an uncertain result never triggers an automatic retry.

When execution becomes idle, fails, completes or is interrupted, an in-progress
record receives one inbox reminder. In the active session, the native UI offers
evidence review, an explicit verdict, or **Keep working**. Finishing requests
separate approval for the final snapshot. The offer is shown once per session;
returning to a session reconciles missed events. An event arriving during another
Kujo dialog is shown after it closes, provided you are still in that session.
If the UI disconnects during presentation, use `/kujo` → Session RunLedger. Closing the
offer or choosing Keep working preserves the in-progress record.
Completion does not imply success. Finalization still requires your selected
verdict and approval; no usage or cost is invented.

Request/reminder/presentation markers survive reload and are bounded to 128 sessions per
project. **Reset tracking requests** clears only those markers after approval,
allowing new requests; canonical run records are preserved. **Recover tracking
journal** handles a stopped writer and refuses live ownership. Disable tracking
to stop new requests. Unload, disable and session cancellation prevent a late
approval from starting a new record; inspect canonical state if a command had
already begun. A host permission dialog may still require dismissal.

This screen does not contact a service or verify credentials. See the

a preflight catalog check is not an atomic server-side version lock.

human approval interface and supply the resulting `approval_id`. OpenCode does

and redirects are refused. Narrow filters when a response exceeds the bound.

limited to the metadata emitted by OpenCode's lifecycle observer.

# Specialist acceptance runner

This document describes the test harness. Recorded results live in the dated
acceptance files; the harness alone does not prove a specialist passed.

`native-specialist-runner.mjs` creates a new owned session with an explicit Kujo
agent and provider/model. It refuses a native fallback to ordinary Build. Each
step specifies its exact Ability/input, expected terminal result and native
permission decision. Before a grant it verifies canonical receipt provenance,
request input, effect identity and absence of persistent permission. Rejection
and cancellation require both a pre-decision invariant and a post-condition.
Provider errors, missing receipts, retries, out-of-scope execution and changed
inputs fail the journey and interrupt only its owned session. Final receipts are
checked again after the host finishes, including late tool execution.

The runner contract tests are part of `npm test`. Fake-host tests verify request
handling and refusal behavior; they do not prove a live specialist passed.

## Understand journey

`KUJO_TEST_JOURNEY=understand` selects the real `kujo-understand` agent, after the
base native checks and a separately approved full-profile selection. It checks:

1. Native Scout rejection leaves no output directory.
2. A separate approved Scout request produces its canonical manifest.
3. An approved Scent dry-run leaves no context artifact. Canonical Ability policy
   still declares output effects, so the adapter does not invent a bypass.
4. A separate approved pack preserves its task, 4,000-token budget and generic
   target and supplies structured context/redaction artifacts.
5. An approved nonexistent-scope request produces a failed canonical receipt,
   with no new target directory or automatic retry.

```sh
KUJO_TEST_RELEASE_DIR=/absolute/candidate \
OPENCODE_BIN=/absolute/isolated/host/bin/opencode \
KUJO_TEST_MODEL=openai/gpt-5.6-sol \
KUJO_TEST_JOURNEY=understand npm run test:native
```

agent, spoof provider identity or choose paid inference implicitly. A provider
403 is failure, not an empty successful journey. Native failure records retain
